text: Splitting a single growing wiki into segmented, topic-distinct wikis (e.g. separating YouTube transcripts from meeting transcripts) narrows the context an agent must search, reducing bloat and confusion and lowering token cost per query.

Data that clashes across sources because it changed over time (e.g. an old policy vs. a new one) causes an agent to answer inconsistently unless claims carry dates and newer entries explicitly supersede older ones, so the system knows which source to trust.

Recurring data pulls (e.g. weekly meeting transcripts or periodic content) should be captured by scheduled automations rather than manual entry, since relying on remembering to add them after the fact causes the knowledge base to silently go stale between sessions.
No public source documents the home speech of Kutch Leva Patels (SKLPC) specifically; available Kutchi descriptions come mostly from Khoja/Memon (Muslim) communities.

Kutch Leva Patel home speech is most likely a Gujarati–Kutchi continuum: one East-Africa survey lists 'Cutchi-speaking Leva Patel (Hindu)', while Wikipedia says Hindus of rural-Kutch descent prefer Gujaratised forms (e.g. 'chhado hane' for 'chhodo have').
SKLPC Saturday School (Kenton, London) teaches Gujarati, not Kutchi.
Kutchi 'how are you?' is 'kien aayo?' (spellings kin/kii/kiy), vs Gujarati 'kem cho?'; 'how' = kien vs kem.
Kutchi pronouns: aaun = I (Gujarati hu), aain = respectful you (Gujarati tame), tu = informal you.
Kutchi 'I am coming / going' = achanto / vinanto (Gujarati aavu chu / jaau chu); 'what' = koro/kuro (Gujarati shu); 'bye' = achija (Gujarati aavjo).
SKLPC UK's annual gathering is the Chovis Gaam Ujamni (Northolt); 2025 drew over 9,000 attendees. 'Chovis gaam' (24 villages) is the community's self-name.
East-African Kutchi uses Swahili loanwords such as saani (plate), boga (vegetables), dizi (banana), sufrio (pot); documented mainly for Muslim Kutchi families, unconfirmed for Leva Patels.
Gujarati distinguishes exclusive 'we' (ame, અમે) from inclusive 'we' (aapne, આપણે).
Gujarati transitive verbs in the past take an ergative subject (me, ene, 'Ba e') and agree with the object, e.g. 'me rotli khadhi' (feminine object).
Gujarati has a future imperative in -je (informal) / -jo (respectful), and 'ne' after a verb softens a command.
Gujarati present tense = verb stem + person marker + copula (chu/che/chiye/cho); future adds -ish/-she/-ishu/-sho.
